text: Everything in SOC Operations and SIEM Fundamentals — alerts, triage, escalation, case notes — happens inside a much larger structure. NIST SP 800-61, the Computer Security Incident Handling Guide, is the framework real SOCs build their incident response programs around, and it's worth knowing by name, because it's the vocabulary job postings and IR plans are written in.

It defines four phases: Preparation, Detection and Analysis, Containment, Eradication and Recovery, and Post-Incident Activity. This isn't academic theory nobody uses. It's the exact framework incident response plans, tabletop exercises, and real job postings for IR analysts are built around. If you can name these four phases and explain what belongs in each one, you can follow almost any real-world incident response conversation.

Preparation is everything a team does before an incident happens: a written IR plan, a trained team, tools and access already in place. Detection and Analysis is where an alert gets formally confirmed as a real incident — the triage process you already know, now at incident scale. Containment, Eradication and Recovery stops the attacker, removes the cause, and restores normal operation. Post-Incident Activity is the lessons-learned review teams skip under deadline pressure, and regret skipping.

This is drawn as a loop, not a line, because every real incident teaches a team something it didn't know before it started. Maybe the plan never said who can take a production server offline at 2 a.m. Maybe a critical log source wasn't actually feeding the SIEM. Post-Incident Activity is where those gaps get written down, and feeding them back into Preparation is what makes the next incident go faster and cleaner than this one did.

Walk the loop once. Preparation: a plan already names who to call, and the team has rehearsed isolating a compromised endpoint. Detection and Analysis: an alert on unusual outbound traffic gets validated against the raw logs and confirmed as a real compromise. Containment, Eradication and Recovery: the team isolates the machine, removes the malware, and restores from a clean image. Post-Incident Activity: the team finds the alert sat untouched for 40 minutes because the on-call rotation wasn't documented — and that fix goes straight back into Preparation, closing the loop. Next up: what Preparation actually contains.
